paragraphs: Trust-region methods optimize a function by restricting each proposed move to a neighborhood where a local approximation is useful. Adaptive versions aim to retain convergence guarantees without requiring conservative estimates of how the problem behaves. This paper identifies a gap between that aim and the theoretical guarantees of existing adaptive methods.

The issue concerns how iteration counts depend on L, the Lipschitz constant of the Hessian, which describes how rapidly curvature can change. The cited TRACE bound scales with L to the power three-halves, whereas the optimal bound scales with its square root. Thus, matching the desired dependence on accuracy alone can conceal an unnecessarily unfavorable dependence on the problem's curvature variation.

The authors introduce a simple modification of a classical trust-region method that achieves the optimal iteration bound up to an additive logarithmic term when finding an approximately stationary point. Their experiments also show competitive performance against ARC and a classical trust-region method. The contribution combines sharper theoretical adaptivity with encouraging practical results.
neurips-2022-a-consistently-adaptive-tru.tldr: A simple adaptive trust-region method attains optimal iteration complexity up to an additive logarithmic term.

paragraphs: An optimization guarantee is useful computationally only if the information required at each step can actually be obtained efficiently. This paper addresses that issue for a previous method for minimizing Lipschitz functions: its attractive efficiency bound relied on an oracle that was not efficiently implementable.

The authors develop a gradient sampling method that preserves the O(ε⁻⁴) efficiency guarantee while using a standard subgradient oracle. The method applies to any Lipschitz function whose value and gradient can be evaluated wherever the function is differentiable. This replaces the problematic information requirement with a more practical one without worsening the stated dependence on the accuracy parameter.

A second contribution targets low-dimensional problems through a cutting-plane algorithm. For functions with smoothness parameter S, including potentially nonconvex functions, its efficiency scales as O(d ε⁻² log S), where d is dimension. Its dependence on ε matches lower bounds from the convex setting. Together, the results distinguish a broadly applicable implementable method from a sharper guarantee available with smoothness and low dimension.
neurips-2022-a-gradient-sampling-method-.tldr: Gradient sampling achieves a previous Lipschitz optimization guarantee with a standard oracle, while a second method gives sharper low-dimensional rates.

paragraphs: Training a large model across multiple accelerators requires deciding how to distribute its computation. Good choices depend on both the model architecture and the available machines, making manual strategy design a specialized systems task. AMP automates this process by searching for effective model-parallel execution strategies.

AMP first identifies valid strategies, then searches them efficiently using a cost model that accounts for differences within the model and the cluster. These differences include uneven layers, heterogeneous accelerators, and varying communication bandwidth. Accounting for them matters because a strategy suited to uniform layers and hardware may use an uneven setup poorly.

On the evaluated public-cloud configurations, AMP finds strategies that match expert tuning for typical clusters. For heterogeneous clusters and heterogeneous model architectures, the reported throughput improvements over state-of-the-art model-parallel systems are 1.54 times and 1.77 times, respectively. These results support using automated, heterogeneity-aware planning to reduce the expertise required for distributed training while improving throughput in the tested uneven settings.
neurips-2022-amp-automatically-finding-m.tldr: AMP automatically searches for model-parallel training strategies that account for uneven model layers, accelerators, and communication bandwidth.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial decisions involve choosing an ordering, and evaluating a candidate ordering can be expensive. This paper develops Bayesian optimization for such permutation problems, with an emphasis on selecting several candidates that can be evaluated in parallel. The goal is to accelerate search when individual evaluations are costly.

The authors first introduce LAW, a batch acquisition method built from determinantal point processes and an acquisition-weighted kernel. This machinery selects a batch through a joint rule rather than treating parallel evaluations as unrelated choices. Applying that framework to permutations yields LAW2ORDER, extending batch Bayesian optimization to an important class of discrete search spaces.

The theoretical analysis establishes sublinear batch cumulative regret and uses it to prove vanishing simple regret. In practical terms, the latter guarantee concerns the quality of the best candidate found as search progresses. The empirical evaluation covers quadratic assignment, flowshop scheduling, the traveling salesman problem, and structure learning. The contribution therefore combines a parallel search mechanism, a permutation-focused application, and a formal convergence guarantee.
neurips-2022-batch-bayesian-optimization.tldr: LAW2ORDER uses batch Bayesian optimization to search permutation spaces in parallel and has a vanishing-simple-regret guarantee.

paragraphs: A sketch compresses a large dataset into a much smaller summary, making queries feasible when retaining all the original data is impractical. This paper asks how to attach trustworthy uncertainty intervals to frequency estimates obtained from such summaries. The target is the number of occurrences of a queried object.

The proposed conformal inference method adapts to the data without requiring the underlying distribution or the internal details of the sketching algorithm. Its confidence intervals have a provable frequentist validity guarantee under exchangeability, meaning that the data's joint distribution does not depend on their ordering. That assumption is central to the guarantee, while detailed distributional modeling is unnecessary.

Although the approach is broadly applicable, the paper concentrates on count-min sketches and a nonlinear variant. It compares the method with frequentist and Bayesian alternatives using simulations, SARS-CoV-2 DNA sequences, and English literature. The contribution is a way to quantify uncertainty around compressed-data frequency queries with a guarantee that is largely independent of the chosen sketch's implementation.
neurips-2022-conformal-frequency-estimat.tldr: A conformal method provides valid frequency-estimation intervals from data sketches under exchangeability, without knowing the distribution or sketch details.

paragraphs: Models such as CLIP learn representations from paired images and text so that the two forms of information can support shared predictions. This paper shows that standard contrastive training does not make those representations interchangeable. Reasoning through the image space or the text space can produce inconsistent downstream predictions.

CyCLIP addresses this mismatch by explicitly encouraging geometric consistency. One constraint symmetrizes similarities between mismatched image-text pairs. Another aligns the similarity between two images with the similarity between their corresponding texts. Together, these constraints make the relationships within and across the two representation spaces more consistent, going beyond simply bringing matched image-text examples together.

The experiments report gains over CLIP of 10%–24% for zero-shot classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet1K, and 10%–27% for robustness under natural distribution shifts. These empirical improvements connect the proposed consistency objective to downstream performance. The paper's broader point is that the geometry linking modalities deserves explicit attention when predictions depend on reasoning across both image and text representations.
neurips-2022-cyclip-cyclic-contrastive-l.tldr: CyCLIP explicitly aligns image-text representation geometry, improving zero-shot classification and robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Recovering a person's three-dimensional pose involves both interpreting observations and understanding how the body relates to its surroundings. This paper approaches the problem through a simulated embodied agent. The agent combines information about its own body and the surrounding scene with external third-person observations to estimate global 3D poses.

The method operates in one stage and causally, rather than requiring future observations. Because two-dimensional observations depend on camera pose, the authors disentangle the camera and construct a multistep projection gradient in global coordinates to guide movement. Physics simulation, prescanned scene geometry, and environmental sensors help the agent navigate and interact with the surrounding environment.

The observation input consists of 2D keypoints, and training can use synthetic datasets derived from human motion databases. Evaluations use H36M and PROX, with high-quality PROX pose estimates reported despite excluding PROX motion sequences from training. The result supports combining visual evidence with simulated body and scene information, while the approach explicitly relies on physics simulation and available scene geometry.
neurips-2022-embodied-scene-aware-human-.tldr: A simulated, scene-aware agent estimates global 3D human poses causally from 2D keypoints and embodied information.

paragraphs: Conventional convolutional networks obtain their hierarchy from layers arranged by a designer. This paper investigates whether a hierarchy can instead emerge from a single unstructured population of spiking neurons. The inspiration is cortical organization, where neighboring regions form maps and neurons responding to similar stimuli cluster together.

The Self-Organizing Neural Sheet model uses local learning rules based on spike timing, together with lateral excitation and inhibition. Connections can grow and disappear dynamically, allowing the model to constrain incoming and outgoing connectivity. Both connection strength and connection length enter the wiring-cost considerations, linking the learned organization to the cost of maintaining connections.

Experiments show that these rules are sufficient for both topographic maps and hierarchical layers to emerge without a predefined architecture or supervision. This is a demonstration of one workable route to such organization, rather than a claim that these rules are uniquely required. The contribution is an architecture-forming learning process: a common pool of neurons can develop structured regions resembling traditional network layers.
neurips-2022-emergence-of-hierarchical-l.tldr: Local learning and dynamic connectivity let hierarchical layers and topographic maps emerge experimentally from an unstructured sheet of spiking neurons.

paragraphs: Initial network weights encode information that can strongly influence subsequent learning. This paper makes that connection mathematically explicit for deep linear networks. By extending a matrix Riccati solution, the authors derive exact descriptions of training with rich prior knowledge across a broad class of tasks and initializations.

The formulas track the network's input-output function, similarities within hidden representations, and the neural tangent kernel over time. They reveal task-independent initializations that change slow nonlinear learning into fast exponential trajectories while reaching a global optimum with identical representational similarity. This separates the path taken during learning from what the structure of internal representations alone might suggest.

The analysis also describes how weights align with task structure as training proceeds. It rigorously explains why earlier solutions captured learning from small initial weights without modeling their fine-grained structure. The authors discuss implications for continual learning, reversal learning, and structured knowledge. The resulting toolkit provides exact insight within deep linear networks into how prior knowledge shapes learning speed and trajectory.
neurips-2022-exact-learning-dynamics-of-.tldr: Exact solutions for deep linear networks reveal how initialization can radically alter learning trajectories and speed.

paragraphs: This paper studies feature learning by changing the variables used to describe a neural network's training objective. Instead of expressing the L2-regularized loss only through weights, it rewrites the loss using the activations produced by each layer on the training set. This shifts attention toward the representations that the network learns.

In that formulation, hidden representations solve attraction-and-repulsion problems and interpolate between input and output representations. They preserve as little input information as needed to construct the next layer's activations. For positively homogeneous nonlinearities, a further reformulation uses representation covariances and yields a partially convex optimization problem over a convex cone.

The covariance view supports a sparsity theorem: any local-minimum loss value can be achieved using at most N(N+1) neurons per hidden layer, where N is the training-set size. An example requiring N²/4 neurons shows that quadratic dependence is necessary in general. Numerical observations in more traditional settings require far fewer than N² neurons, distinguishing worst-case representational requirements from the observed behavior of those examples.
neurips-2022-feature-learning-in-l-2-reg.tldr: Rewriting regularized neural-network losses in terms of representations reveals feature-learning structure and quadratic worst-case bounds on hidden-layer width.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation identifies pixels belonging to a new class using only a few annotated examples. Many methods accomplish this through elaborate decoders that match pixels between support and query images. FPTrans returns to a simpler arrangement: a feature extractor followed by a linear classification head whose class-representing vectors are called proxies.

To make that simple head effective, FPTrans allows query features to interact with support features throughout the feature extractor using transformer prompts. It also represents the background through multiple local proxies. This matters because background regions need not form one coherent category and may contain objects that would be foreground for another novel class.

Both mechanisms fit into a vision transformer through prompting. Once the model has learned features and proxies, segmentation uses their cosine similarity directly. The reported accuracy is competitive with state-of-the-art methods that use complex decoders. The finding supports investing in informative features and representative class vectors as a way to obtain strong few-shot segmentation within a straightforward prediction framework.
neurips-2022-feature-proxy-transformer-f.tldr: FPTrans combines support-aware transformer features with class proxies to achieve competitive few-shot segmentation using a simple prediction head.

paragraphs: Some machine-learning optimization problems involve competing minimization and maximization objectives on curved spaces. Algorithms for ordinary Euclidean spaces are well studied, but their guarantees do not automatically transfer to Riemannian manifolds. This paper asks whether curved geometry necessarily imposes a worse convergence rate for convex-concave problems.

The authors analyze Riemannian corrected extragradient, or RCEG. For geodesically strongly convex-concave problems, they prove linear convergence of the last iterate, matching the Euclidean rate. A last-iterate guarantee concerns the algorithm's current solution directly. The result establishes that a convergence-rate gap is not unavoidable in this setting.

The work also extends to stochastic and nonsmooth cases. RCEG and Riemannian gradient ascent-descent respectively achieve near-optimal rates, with factors that depend on manifold curvature. Experiments on robust principal component analysis demonstrate RCEG's effectiveness for a concrete application. The findings therefore combine a matching rate under strong geometric convexity-concavity with broader guarantees that still explicitly account for the influence of curved geometry.
neurips-2022-first-order-algorithms-for-.tldr: Riemannian corrected extragradient matches Euclidean linear convergence in the geodesically strongly convex-concave setting.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization converts a trained network to a lower-precision representation. Existing approaches often divide the network into smaller parts and quantize them sequentially, giving limited attention to dependencies between parts. Network-Wise Quantization instead treats those inter-layer dependencies as a central part of the optimization problem.

Optimizing across the network creates a larger combinatorial problem because quantized values are discrete. The method addresses overfitting with activation regularization, which controls activation distributions. It also introduces Annealing Softmax for weights and Annealing Mixup for activations, progressively moving from continuous representations toward discrete ones so that the quantization process can be optimized more gradually.

The experiments report a 20.24% improvement over previous state-of-the-art results for the challenging setting of 2-bit MobileNetV2 on ImageNet. Separately, the method achieves competitive results using only 10% of the computation cost of previous work. These findings suggest that coordinating quantization across layers can substantially improve extremely low-bit networks while also offering an economical computation setting.
neurips-2022-leveraging-inter-layer-depe.tldr: Network-Wise Quantization coordinates layers and gradually discretizes weights and activations to improve low-bit post-training quantization.

paragraphs: Optimal transport finds low-cost ways to match distributions or collections of points. Its growing use in machine learning creates pressure for methods that can handle millions of points. This paper examines low-rank optimal transport as an approach to making such matching computations more scalable.

Low-rank optimal transport restricts the allowed couplings, or matching plans, to those with low nonnegative rank. This structural restriction yields linear-time algorithms in cases of interest and can fit into more complex transport pipelines. The paper positions this approach alongside entropic regularization, emphasizing that computational promise must be assessed together with statistical and practical properties.

The authors address approximation, statistical complexity, connections to other methods, and practical questions involving debiasing, hyperparameter selection, and initialization. These are consequential because a scalable solver needs a well-understood relationship to the intended matching problem and usable procedures for choosing its settings. The contribution is a broader foundation for evaluating and using low-rank transport, rather than computational scalability considered in isolation.
neurips-2022-low-rank-optimal-transport-.tldr: The paper develops theoretical and practical foundations for low-rank optimal transport as a scalable matching approach.

paragraphs: A traffic participant can have several plausible futures, so motion prediction must represent multiple possible behaviors. The paper identifies drawbacks in two existing strategies: predicting every motion mode from one latent feature can slow convergence, while searching dense destination candidates can make performance depend heavily on candidate density.

Motion Transformer, or MTR, jointly learns where broad intentions are located and how detailed movements should be refined. It introduces a small collection of learnable motion-query pairs that incorporate spatial intention priors. Each pair handles prediction and refinement for a particular motion mode, giving different possible futures distinct responsibilities within the model.

This division stabilizes training and supports better multimodal predictions in the reported experiments. MTR achieves state-of-the-art results on both marginal and joint motion prediction challenges and ranks first on the cited Waymo Open Motion Dataset leaderboards. The approach matters because it coordinates broad behavioral alternatives with local trajectory detail through a compact learned set of queries.
neurips-2022-motion-transformer-with-glo.tldr: MTR assigns learnable query pairs to distinct motion modes, jointly locating intentions and refining trajectories.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, their behavior can be more structured than an arbitrary adversarial environment. This paper studies whether that structure permits lower regret, a measure of accumulated missed payoff opportunities. It considers variationally stable continuous games, a class including convex-concave and monotone games, with noisy payoff-gradient estimates.

The kind of noise is decisive. With additive noise, the game setting and the fully adversarial setting have similar regret guarantees. With multiplicative noise, however, the authors show that learners can achieve constant regret. Their optimistic gradient method uses different learning-rate schedules for extrapolation and updating, choosing those schedules according to the noise profile.

To avoid delicate manual tuning, the paper also proposes a fully adaptive method that transitions smoothly between worst-case and best-case regret guarantees. The results explain when interaction among optimizing agents can yield substantially stronger guarantees despite noisy feedback. In particular, constant regret is tied to the stated game and noise setting; the adaptive contribution addresses how to exploit favorable conditions without manually selecting the required schedules.
neurips-2022-no-regret-learning-in-games.tldr: Separating extrapolation and update learning rates enables constant regret under multiplicative noise in the studied stable games.

paragraphs: Network depth places a constraint on the lowest theoretical latency because successive layers create a chain of dependent computations. This paper asks whether strong recognition performance can be achieved with relatively few such stages. Its proposed networks use parallel subnetworks to reduce depth while retaining high predictive performance.

The central architectural choice is to expand through parallel substructures rather than repeatedly adding successive layers. The authors also analyze scaling rules for this design, showing how performance can increase while depth remains fixed. This makes the arrangement of computation an explicit part of the tradeoff between recognition quality and potential latency.

A depth-12 network achieves top-1 accuracy above 80% on ImageNet, 96% on CIFAR10, and 81% on CIFAR100. A depth-12 backbone also achieves 48% average precision on MS-COCO. The paper provides a proof of concept for low-latency recognition systems using these networks. Together, these results demonstrate that the tested recognition tasks can support high performance with shallow sequential depth and substantial parallel structure.
neurips-2022-non-deep-networks-01c9f469b.tldr: Parallel subnetworks enable strong image recognition with only 12 layers of depth and offer a route toward low-latency systems.

paragraphs: Detecting recurring sequences in neural recordings helps researchers identify patterns of neural activity. Existing methods discussed in this paper require the whole dataset in memory and repeated passes through it. They also require advance knowledge of the number of sequence types, which is difficult when recordings grow and future patterns are unknown.

The proposed hierarchical Dirichlet point process handles sequence detection sequentially and without supervision. Particle filters support online inference, allowing the model to work through arriving observations rather than repeatedly processing the entire dataset. A Dirichlet prior lets it introduce additional sequence types as needed, removing the requirement to fix their number beforehand.

The authors demonstrate these advantages on synthetic data and recordings from the songbird higher vocal center and rodent hippocampus. The two changes address complementary obstacles: sequential inference accommodates expanding data, while flexible sequence-type creation accommodates expanding pattern diversity. The contribution is therefore an online detection framework designed for situations where neither the final dataset nor the full set of sequence types is known in advance.
neurips-2022-online-neural-sequence-dete.tldr: A hierarchical Dirichlet point process detects neural sequences online and adds new sequence types as needed.

paragraphs: The paper establishes a connection between differential privacy and resistance to corrupted data. Private algorithms that are accurate with very high probability automatically retain accuracy when an adversary corrupts a constant fraction of their samples. The high-success-probability condition is essential to the stated implication.

The authors use this connection to investigate sparse mean estimation. Assuming the Brennan-Bresler secret-leakage planted clique conjecture, they derive a tradeoff among computational efficiency, privacy leakage, and success probability. They then use the Sum-of-Squares method to match that tradeoff up to polylogarithmic factors across a polynomially large range of parameters.

They also construct exponential-time private mechanisms that need fewer samples than efficient algorithms must use under the computational premise, establishing an information-computation gap. Further evidence concerns parity learning and multivariate Gaussian mean estimation. The findings show how a privacy guarantee, combined with unusually reliable accuracy, can impose robustness and thereby connect private estimation to computationally difficult statistical problems. This makes success probability part of the computational tradeoff itself.
neurips-2022-privacy-induces-robustness-.tldr: Highly reliable private algorithms inherit robustness, yielding conditional computational tradeoffs and new algorithms for sparse mean estimation.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process decoders are appealing because they marginalize over nonlinear functions instead of committing to a single decoder function. In practice, these models can be expensive and difficult to train. This paper revisits active-set approximations as a way to make their training more robust and computationally manageable.

The authors develop a stochastic estimate of the log-marginal likelihood using connections to cross-validation. They then introduce a computationally efficient approximation to that estimate, producing the stochastic active sets method, or SAS. The approach changes how the training objective is estimated, offering another route to scaling Gaussian-process decoders alongside existing inducing-point and variational techniques.

The reported results show substantially more robust training with lower computational cost. SAS-GP scales to many datapoints, produces a more structured latent space, and learns better representations than variational autoencoders in the demonstrated comparisons. These findings matter because they address both the practical difficulty of fitting GP decoders and the quality of the representations obtained, two obstacles to their wider use.
neurips-2022-revisiting-active-sets-for-.tldr: Stochastic active sets make Gaussian-process decoder training cheaper and more robust while improving the demonstrated latent representations.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization depends on how examples are selected as well as on the update rule. This paper analyzes that choice for smooth finite-sum minimax problems, where one variable is minimized while another is maximized. It shows that sampling without replacement gives faster convergence for many of the algorithms studied.

For strongly convex-strongly concave objectives, the authors analyze gradient descent-ascent and the proximal point method. A unified treatment covers random reshuffling, which changes the order every epoch, and shuffle once, which randomizes the order only initially. They establish tight convergence rates for both and show improvements over uniform sampling with replacement.

The analysis extends beyond convexity to smooth nonconvex-nonconcave objectives satisfying a two-sided Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality. It also handles adversarial manipulation of data order and recovers tight rates for incremental gradient updates with no shuffling. The results make data order a theoretically consequential algorithmic choice, while tying the faster rates to explicit structural conditions on the objective.
neurips-2022-sampling-without-replacemen.tldr: Without-replacement sampling yields provably faster convergence for several minimax algorithms under the studied structural conditions.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to adapt to new tasks from few examples, but training the meta-learner can itself require many tasks. This becomes a bottleneck when tasks are expensive or difficult to construct. The paper addresses that shortage by augmenting the distribution of available training tasks.

Existing augmentation methods can depend on domain-specific knowledge, making them difficult to transfer. The authors also find empirically that domain-agnostic Manifold Mixup approaches are ineffective in non-image domains. Their alternative, Meta-Interpolation, uses expressive neural set functions and bilevel optimization to construct interpolated tasks and make the training-task distribution denser.

Experiments cover eight datasets across image classification, molecular property prediction, text classification, and speech recognition. Meta-Interpolation consistently outperforms the relevant baselines in those evaluations. A theoretical result also shows that set-function task interpolation regularizes the meta-learner to improve generalization. The contribution combines a method designed to work across domains with empirical breadth and a theoretical explanation for why interpolating tasks can help when relatively few original tasks are available.
neurips-2022-set-based-meta-interpolatio.tldr: Meta-Interpolation learns domain-agnostic task augmentations that improve few-task meta-learning across the evaluated domains.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional scenes contain many background points, while object detection mainly needs information about foreground objects. This paper finds that existing sparse 3D convolutional networks still perform substantial redundant computation. Their downsampling operations can amplify that redundancy, increasing the cost of processing regions that contribute little to detection.

Spatial pruned sparse convolution addresses this by dynamically selecting important spatial areas for computation. The authors provide variants for both submanifold and regular sparse convolutions. Empirically, feature magnitude serves as a useful cue for identifying important areas, avoiding the heavy computation associated with learning-based selection methods.

The operators can be inserted into existing sparse 3D convolutional networks without additional architectural modifications. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes show reductions of more than 50% in GFLOPs without compromising detection performance. These results indicate that spatial selection can remove substantial computation from already sparse networks. The key distinction is that spatial sparsity alone does not eliminate redundancy among the points that a network still processes.
neurips-2022-spatial-pruned-sparse-convo.tldr: Spatially pruned sparse convolutions cut GFLOPs by more than half in the reported 3D detection experiments without reducing performance.

paragraphs: A classifier can be accurate while still assigning misleading confidence to its predictions. This paper studies uncertainty when each example has multiple views, an area less explored than uncertainty for a single input modality. It aims to improve both ordinary classification and detection of examples from outside the training domain.

The proposed framework assigns each view its own uncertainty-aware classifier, then combines their predictions through a principled aggregation method. This makes uncertainty part of the processing of individual views as well as the final prediction. The design treats the available views as multiple sources of predictive evidence whose contributions must be combined carefully.

Experiments on real-world datasets show an accurate and well-calibrated classifier, meaning its confidence better reflects its predictive reliability. The approach predominantly outperforms the tested multi-view baselines in expected calibration error, noise robustness, and accuracy for in-domain classification and out-of-domain detection. These findings support jointly considering multiple views when estimating uncertainty, with the reported advantage applying to the evaluated methods and datasets.
neurips-2022-uncertainty-estimation-for-.tldr: Combining uncertainty-aware classifiers across views improves calibration, robustness, and classification in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: When benchmark accuracy becomes very high, the meaning of the remaining errors becomes increasingly important. This paper manually examines and categorizes every remaining mistake made by several leading models on ImageNet's multi-label subset evaluation. In that setting, the best models considered exceed 97% top-1 accuracy.

The review finds that nearly half of the supposed mistakes are actually valid predictions missing from the accepted labels. Adding those valid labels shows that the existing evaluation understates model performance. At the same time, about 40% of the reviewed mistakes are plainly incorrect to human reviewers, revealing substantial recognizable failures among the remaining errors.

The authors provide an updated multi-label evaluation set and ImageNet-Major, a collection of 68 obvious-error examples. The latter targets cases where they argue models should perform almost perfectly but remain far from that standard. These resources separate incomplete annotation from clear recognition failure, making future benchmark gains easier to interpret and directing attention toward errors that remain meaningful despite very high overall accuracy.
neurips-2022-when-does-dough-become-a-ba.tldr: Manual review reveals many apparent ImageNet errors are valid predictions, while a curated 68-example set exposes obvious remaining failures.
